ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: diplomacy
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: A good turn big enough leaves a debt of honor between the colony and a people, either way. The colony can call in what it is owed, and the peoples call in what the colony owes them when the world shows they are in need. A truce keeps a people at war away for a season or a year, and a pact with a friend brings their fighters or their trade.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Call a debt in while their head thinks well of the colony: at a regard of 20 or more they always honor it.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description:
The colony's dealings with the peoples around it are kept as ties between two sides: what one owes the other, what was promised, what is held against whom. A town's card on the region map shows the debts of honor between its people and the colony and what the colony can do, each greyed with why not. The region window's Peoples has all of it, what is owed each way at its top and a card for each people, and its Here and away has who is here from outside and who of the colony's people is away. The map's Stance and ties lens draws each debt as a dotted line from home, a pact as a solid line and a truce as a dashed one; the Threats lens dims a town whose people hold a truce with the colony.
When the colony does a people a good turn of size 10 or more in their memory, they owe the colony a debt of honor for it, and the letter that tells of it says so (or, when no letter comes, the evening's news). A notable helped in person, freed or tended or well hosted, owes the colonist who did it. When a people does the colony a good turn of that size (their fighters in a fight, relief, medicine sent when asked by letter, lessons, a raiders' camp struck), the colony owes them.
Once a season at a home, the colony can hold a feast with guests: "Hold a feast for them" on a people's card, "Invite to a feast" on a notable's, the feast row at the top of the calendar, or the steward's suggestion, the council's question when the stores are full, the land is quiet and a notable who thinks 20 or more of the colony lives within reach. Up to three notables of peoples at peace who live within three days' travel and think 0 or more of the colony are invited by letter or call, and a prize may be set aside from the stores (art, or a weapon or clothes of good quality or better). Each answers by their regard, the road and whether what their people hope for is offered: a hunt for a tribe, a hunt or wrestling in the middle ages, a race or a shooting match for an industrial people, wrestling or a game at the tables for spacers, a fine meal and music for the Empire (its best player plays for them where the colony has an instrument). With Ideology their faith's own feast is named in their letter. The day is the first fine one after the last of them can arrive, within two more days, and shows on the calendar and in This week; the feast's Event card follows it, and "Call it off" there before the guests come lowers the regard of each who said yes by 5. By the colony's age it is a gift feast, a feast in the hall, a banquet or a gala.
On the day each guest walks in with one or two of their people and waits by the gate. From noon up to four contests are held on the map, an outdoor one only in fine weather and before six in the evening: wrestling (up to three bouts in a ring by the gate by the sparring rules, eight swings each or until one yields to the pain; the most bouts won), a race from the gate to a marker and back (the first home; children run races and take part in nothing else), a hunt of safe game marked on the colony's land for up to three hours (the most kills), a game at the colony's tables as the game's own recreation (chess, poker, billiards, horseshoes, hoopstone or a mod's game, won by its skill and some luck), and a shooting match only where a mod gives targets (five shots each, the most hits). The feast is the colony's gathering in the evening with the guests at its table; the one who won the most is named champion of the day and the prize is carried to them (a guest takes it home). The guests stay the night in the colony's beds (guest beds first) or on the floor, and go home at first light. Their welcome moves their regard: a meal at the colony's table (an empty plate is a slight their people remember), a fine one for the Empire, what they hoped for, the contests, the prize, a bed; a good welcome is a good turn their people remember, and their head thinks better of the colony too. A bout's blow goes in harder than meant about one time in 25, never on a child, someone with child or anyone hurt in the last three days; a hunted beast may turn on its hunter at the game's own chance; about one guest night in 15, more with a hot temper, words after the feast turn into a fistfight with one of the colony's. When the colony's own go to a neighbour's feast, what they won there is told when they come home.
A marriage alliance binds the colony to a people through two of its own: one of the colony's and one of theirs, a notable (their heir, their envoy, a face the colony knows) or a son or daughter of a town head's house. A match comes three ways: "Speak for a match" when talking with someone of theirs at the colony (two who courted their way to lovers speak for themselves), a letter proposing one ("Seek a match" on a people's card, "Propose a match" on a notable's, which also says who of the colony's would fit), or their own offer by letter, once a year at most from a people at peace whose head thinks 40 or more of the colony. Who may marry is the game's own rule: both grown (18 or more), each drawn to the other, not kin, free to take a spouse by their faith (unmarried, or a faith that allows more), not promised elsewhere, and the Empire's titled nobles only to a titled colonist. The colonist is asked first: with a lover here, children they would leave behind or a dislike of the one chosen they are against it, and once their people say yes the council hears the objection before anything is settled (pressed all the same, it weighs on the colonist for twenty days; withdrawn, their people feel turned down). They agree by their head's regard (never below 0, much likelier for two lovers), and where the couple lives is chosen each time: either side may move. Gifts go both ways at the gate (theirs by their ways: a tribe's goods, gold from the middle ages and the Empire, silver from the rest; the colony's silver, up to the same worth, 100 to 250 by their town's fortune).
If theirs comes to the colony, their kin come on the day as the wedding's guests (up to two of their notables, each with a retinue), the one to be married joins the colony at the gate, and the game's own ceremony marries the two before the evening while the guests watch; the guests sit at the evening's feast and go home at first light. If the colony's own goes to them, the one they marry and one of their kin walk up to the gate, the colonist walks out to them and leaves for good as one of their people, and their letter tells of the wedding at their town. The wedding makes the marriage alliance: their people remember it as a good turn (15), and while it holds their notables think 15 better of the colony, their kin send a small gift each season, they write when a raiders' camp is set against the colony, and it stands as a defense pact between the two (one pact, not two, kept running while the marriage holds; never with the Empire, which makes no pacts). A child of the two keeps it after a spouse's death; with none it ends. If the couple part it ends and their regard falls. A spouse wronged by the colony (killed by a colonist's hand, executed, imprisoned, enslaved, sold or banished) breaks it, and the pact with it: the gravest wrong their people remember (30), and their head holds a grudge against the colony that the next head takes up. One of theirs who dies at the colony costs some regard when sheltered and tended, much more in the open or untended. Diplomatic Marriage+'s own alliance shows on the pages as the mod's, and Rimfolk adds nothing to it.
Wards. A people at peace whose head thinks 30 or more of the colony may offer a youth of one of their notables' houses to live at the colony for a year, at most once a year and a season apart at each home, while someone at the home has 10 or more in a skill; the colony may also ask by letter ("Ask for a ward" on their card, picking the skill to learn). The ward is a child of 9 to 12 where the game has children, else 14 to 19. They walk in with one of their kin, who leaves them at the gate, and live at the colony as the game's lodger: in the Quests tab, on the colonist bar, working with everyone else, in need of a bed of their own. Their guardian, the colonist with the most of the skill (or one picked on the ward's card), teaches them an hour a day by day, when both are free and together; a child with Biotech learns at the game's own lessons instead. Their card says how they are (homesick, settling in, happy, from their mood and their first ten days), what they have learned, where they sleep, and whether they went hungry or were hurt. At the year's end their kin come to the gate, the ward walks out to them, and the year is reckoned: taught (a lesson on half the days), fed (hungry on a tenth of the days at most), unhurt, content. A fine year raises their head's regard by 20 and leaves their people owing the colony a debt of honor, a good one by 12, a fair one by 4, and a poor one costs 10 and is remembered as a slight. A ward hurt or killed in the colony's care grieves their people, little if the colony sheltered them and much in the open, and a death at a colonist's hand is a feud. The ward remembers the year: grown, and one day an heir or a head of their people, they still think better or worse of the colony for it. In the colony's own words by its age a ward is fostering with the other clan, a ward at their hall, an apprentice exchange or an exchange posting; by their ways, a child raised among them, a youth in their household, an apprenticeship under contract, a posting on agreed terms.
The colony's own youth. "Offer a youth" on a people's card writes to their head about a youth of the home (14 to 19, or 10 to 19 where the game has children). Taken in, the youth sets out by caravan for their nearest town with food for the road and lives there a year, a lent colonist whose work is lost to the colony. Every ten days a letter comes home, and the town's notables think better of the colony. They come home with what that people are good at by their ways (a tribe's beasts and plants, the middle ages' crafts and the sword, the machine age's building and medicine, the spacers' learning and medicine), about a lesson's worth of practice a day spent there, and a friend among the town's notables; "Call home" on their card brings them back sooner. The Empire takes a youth as a page in a titled household instead, for regard alone: no skill is learned there.
Hostages. A truce's price can be a hostage either way, "a hostage from them" or one of the colony's by name, and so can a defense pact's terms; a hostage of theirs makes them less willing to agree, one of the colony's more. Hostages are grown, 18 or more: children are never hostages. Theirs, one of their notable's kin, walks in to the gate once the terms are sworn and lives at the colony as its lodger for the term (a people at war with the colony only where a people at peace with both can vouch for them on the road); the colony's sets out by caravan for their town and lives there. When the truce ends, or a pact's year is out (even when the pact is kept another year, which may ask for new hostages of its own), both go home, and their people remember the colony returned theirs. This week shows each one under way, and every decision about one.
Council tasks. Eight offices can each take one task at a time at their home: set on the Decrees page's row for the office, on the officer's card, or from a people's card ("Council task...", the target first, then the office). The council's question names who does it, what each step is and what it risks. By the colony's age the tasks are the elders' errands, the council's offices, the committee's portfolios or the board's remits. The speaker wins over a town's head: a letter every four to six days (a call where the colony has a working console and their people are industrial or later), an invitation once, a visit once a season; each letter warms the head by the speaker's Social (1 to 6, a visit three times that, half again from a titled head to a titled officer), and at a regard of 60 their people offer a defense pact against an enemy of both, else a trade pact, else owe the colony a favor. The quartermaster opens a trade with a town's trader the same way, by Social and Intellectual, and can send samples of the colony's surplus fetched from the gate; when it is open, their people offer a trade pact, or send their caravan within three days. The marshal walks the edges at dawn every other day for a season (a raiders' camp being set up nearby is seen three times in five on a walk), or visits a defense pact partner to drill their fighters (their band comes a fifth stronger for a season). The physician takes up to six of the colony's medicine to a town with a sickness running and spends a day with their sick; their people remember it, and one visit in five the sickness comes home with one of the party. The warden of guests writes to the people holding one of the colony's (after two letters their word on a price comes to the gate, lower for each letter and for Social, down to half), or to a people whose kin are in the colony's cells (while the warden writes, their offers come in half the time and a quarter higher). The chaplain keeps the faith with a head of the colony's faith (their regard, and the believers at home a little surer for each kind answer) or speaks for it to one of another (their certainty shaken a little, never below a fifth, never a conversion). The steward writes to prepare a feast for a people and the council plans it; their guests' welcome counts half again. A visit is a journey of the journey planner for the next morning: the officer and a companion go by caravan, stay a day and come home, and their work waits. At most one officer of a home is away at a time, each office visits once a season, and the roads are the world's own. Each task's last step and the next show on the officer's card, under the office's row and in Here and away, never as a time left; This week lists every task under way and asks when a visit or a feast waits to be planned. A task with letters gives up after a year; one for a season ends after it.
The keeper of secrets. A seat of Social and Intellectual that opens at six voters. While it is filled, the colony's own secrets slip half as often. After dark, with guests on the colony's land, the keeper walks with them a while. Sounding out someone of another people face to face ("Sound out", the keeper's only), the keeper's task with a chosen notable (talks with their people when they come by, a paid informer met at the gate for 60 to 120 silver, a visit), and the walk after dark may learn something a notable of theirs keeps quiet: a debt, a cut of every caravan, raiders paid off, grain hidden, an heir who isn't who the town thinks, a raider's past, an illness, a lover. Each step is the keeper's Social and Intellectual against the notable's (35% when even, from a tenth to four in five, more on a visit or from an informer), and one step in ten the keeper is found out: the notable thinks 15 less of the colony and 25 less of the keeper, and says so at their next meeting. The colony knows at most twenty such secrets at once, each for a year. A secret can be pressed by letter from the notable's card, or face to face when they visit: they pay 100 silver a weight to keep it quiet (likelier the heavier it is and the better they think of the colony), or refuse, and the colony tells it; either way they think less of the colony, and a secret told costs 30 more and is remembered by their people as the colony's scheme.
Fealty. The colony can swear fealty to a stronger neighbor: a people at peace with goodwill 40 or more and two towns or more within reach, never the Empire, whose titles and permits are its own fealty (a colonist holding one of its titles shows on its card as sworn to it, its permits their protection). "Swear fealty..." on a people's card shows their terms by their ways and what the oath may cost, then a letter or call to their head; they take it half the time at a mean of 40 between their goodwill and their head's regard, nearly always among close friends. A people may also offer its protection to a colony raided twice in a season with five fighters or fewer, at most once a year. Agreed, their head or someone who speaks for them comes to the gate with a guard. One of the colony's sworn to vengeance on them, a proud colonist, or a devout one of another faith first has their say before the council, which can swear all the same or send them home; then the speaker walks out and swears by their rite. By the colony's age the oath is tribute to a stronger clan, fealty and tribute, a protectorate or a charter; by theirs, protection for tribute, an oath of fealty and levies, a company town and a union's dues, or a corporate accord. Each season their collector comes to the gate by day and the tribute is carried out to them: 150 silver's worth for a poor colony, 600 at most (at 150,000 wealth), in silver when the stores hold it, else in the most plentiful goods. What the stores can't cover is owed ("Send what is owed" on the oath's card, or the quartermaster's dues), and still owed at the next season's day the oath breaks: 20 goodwill, and they remember the tribute short. When a town of theirs within reach is attacked (a war near it, or Faction Territories' invasion), their letter calls the colony's levies, two fighters by caravan within five days, to fight beside them there as a pact partner's call is answered; refused or not sent, 10 goodwill, and the oath stands. When a home is raided by a people, their band comes without a call, half the threat, at most once a season and nine times in ten, never against their own friends; a season in which they failed lets the colony leave without blame. Renouncing is the council's question: their grudge, 30 goodwill and the deed, unless they failed this season. Their enemies stay their own business: nothing moves the colony's goodwill with anyone else.
Vassals. The colony's own vassals are its hamlet once it swore, and up to two struggling towns within reach (under 20 prosperity for 30 days, their people at peace with the colony and at war with someone else, never the Empire's) that ask for its protection, one ask a year at most. Each vassal's head is a notable who writes, and how they think of the colony shows on the town's card with what moved it lately. At harvest a vassal's carter brings produce to the gate, six tenths of it, as it comes, or eight fifths, as the council sets it on the town's card (light warms their head; heavy costs 3 goodwill each season and their head's regard). The quartermaster's task "collect the dues" writes to a vassal's head for a season's dues (40 to 100 silver by its fortune, less or more by the council's level), which their carter brings to the gate; in a hard season half, and explained. While a threat is on a home the council may call a vassal's levies ("Call their levies" on the town's card, or the alert), their people's band at a third of the threat, once a season; each of theirs who falls costs 6 of their head's regard, 20 at most. Once a season at most a vassal asks something: food or medicine in a hard season, the colony's judgment in a quarrel with a neighboring town (siding with them pleases their head and costs the neighbor's people 5 goodwill, and the other way round), or a camp of the colony's enemies near them broken within a season. Their head sour (regard -20 or lower) for a season asks to be released; released, a protected town goes its own way and the hamlet stands under the colony's protection as before it swore; refused, they break away, the tie broken and 15 goodwill. Faction Territories' vassals are that mod's own: Rimfolk gives each outpost a head of its first people (the town's own head when it was made from a town the notables knew), who writes, thinks of the colony and asks, including the colony's fighters when the mod's invasion comes against it (joined through the mod's own "Join fight"); it takes no tribute or levies from them, and their points, purchases and tribute stay the mod's.
House renown. Two or more of the colony's people of one family name who are family to each other are a house of the colony (twelve at most, kept two years after the last of them leaves, longer while a tie names one of them); the founding families of the towns are the region's. A house's renown is never spent and never kept as a number: it is read from what its people did that the world saw (contests won at feasts, marriages into other peoples' houses, wards fostered well, seasons abroad as the colony's youth, envoy or hostage, truces sworn as its speaker, the council's business carried abroad, what the peoples remember of them by name, the colony's names for them, years in office, the Empire's titles, notables who think well of them), and from the colony's own oaths kept and broken, which each of its houses shares; a region's house from its founding, its head's place, its town's fortune and its ties with the colony. A deed counts in full for a year, then a tenth less each season down to three tenths. At 10 a house's name is known in a town nearby, at 30 across the region, at 60 among every people within reach, at -15 for the wrong things, each told in the ways of whoever speaks of it (told at the fires, sung in the halls, in the papers, carried on every channel; by the Empire's people in the court's, spoken of with honor in the noble houses). What most of it came from is what it is known for, in the house's own age's words: fighters, healers, hosts, traders, makers or the faithful. When one of the colony's houses moves a band the news says so, and as its name carries further or fades from the talk one of its people at home, awake, says so where they stand. Its House card (People → Houses, or a colonist's card) shows how far its name carries and for what, the deeds it came from, who knows it, its marriages, wards and feuds, and its story. Notables think up to 15 better of a renowned house's people (up to 10 worse of an infamous one's), good words for them count up to half again, matches with them are offered and accepted up to twice as readily, what a house is known for draws the world's events of that kind up to three quarters more often (challengers to fighters, the sick and the hurt to healers, guests to hosts, the far market to traders, work remembered to makers, pilgrims to the faithful; the champion challenges its fighter more often than not), and a feast's guests answer a house known for hosting up to three tenths more readily.
Against their nature. Some of what diplomacy asks goes against a colonist's nature (the sides of their character on their card), and it builds the heart's own strain, with no mood of its own: the oath of fealty weighs on the one who swears it at the gate, if proud; a truce or a pact the colony breaks, on whoever struck the blow, took the captive or made the sale that broke it, or on the speaker who sent the colony's refusal of a pact's call, if trusting; a hostage of the colony's, on the hostage as they walk off the map, if timid, and on their close kin there to see them go, if warm; a youth sent away as a ward, on the parents there to see them go, if warm; a match pressed over the colonist's objection, on them, always; a challenger turned away, on the colony's champion, if proud or hot-tempered, and a challenge faced, on the champion, if timid; a season away as envoy or hostage, on the one who goes, if set in their ways; asking more for a captive whose family waits, on the speaker, and on the captive's close kin among the colony there, if warm; a truce with a people someone swore vengeance on, on the avenger at that home, always. The further past where a side shows (30) they are, the more: up to 12 strain, at least 8 for what weighs on anyone, about 5 just past it, scaled as life's pressures are (half on gentle, 0.85 on normal, half again on demanding, down to three quarters when they are near breaking), within the heart's caps for the day. What suits their nature eases them instead: a season away eases the curious, up to 6. One act a day for each colonist. The heart's page says what they did, against what side of them, and that a quiet evening with friends would help; the colony's news tells it; the council's question names it before an answer that would ask it (the speaker's pride for an oath, the avenger's vengeance for a truce, the colonist's heart for a match pressed, the champion's nature for a challenge). An oath sworn may humble a proud one (half the time), and the same act against the same side twice within a year may change them: a word broken twice makes a trusting one warier, a challenge faced twice makes a timid one bolder, a second season away makes one set in their ways more open.

li.heading: Debts of honor
li.text: One debt is open each way between a people and each colony; a new good turn while one is open renews it. A notable's personal debts to single colonists are twelve at most, the oldest let go first. A debt nobody asks for is let go two years (120 days) after the good turn that made or renewed it. The words for a debt follow both sides' ages: the colony's word by its own age, and the way it is done among them by theirs.

table.li: Age | The colony's word | Their way
Tribal | a debt of the hearth | a gift owed back
Medieval | a debt of honor | a pledge given by hand
Industrial | an IOU | a favor on the books
Spacer | a ledger entry | credit owed

li.after: A trade, a gift or a payment leaves no debt: those are paid for already. Nor does the colony keeping its word when they call one in.

li.heading: Calling a debt in
li.text: The colony calls one in by a letter or a call to their head (or to the notable who owes it in person), from the region map's town panel or the letters, or face to face with someone of theirs at the colony ("Ask a favor of their people" when talking with them). What they can do now is listed, each greyed with why not: a load of goods (food, medicine, wood, steel or silver by their ways, about 400 silver's worth from a steady town, three quarters of that from a struggling one, a quarter more from a flourishing one), brought by their porters or with the answer's messenger; a word for the colony with a third people they are on good terms with (10 goodwill, said in that people's own letter); a colonist of the colony they hold, set down at the edge of the colony's land to walk home; their help toward peace with a people at war with the colony, a promise kept for a year that their truce answer reads as if that people thought 20 better of the colony; or, while a threat is on a home, their fighters, whose band walks in some hours later as a defense partner's does.

table.li: Their head's regard of the colony | They honor it
20 or more | always
0 to 19 | seven times in ten
below 0 | four times in ten

li.after: A refusal is their answer, and the colony remembers it against them. A debt is not called in across a war.

li.heading: When they call one in
li.text: A people the colony owes looks at it once a day and calls it in about once in 90 days, but only when the world shows a need, and at most once a season. Medicine while a sickness runs among them, food in a famine: their letter, answered by carrying it out to their messenger at the colony's gate, or refused. Hands at their harvest, or a roof for their homeless: the harvest and refugee missions, asked by them, with the debt named in the letter. The colony's word on their side in a blood feud or a contested seat: the speaker writes it to their head. Refused, or left unanswered for three days (a mission until it ends), the debt is broken: they remember it, and lose 5 goodwill toward the colony. Answered, they remember that the colony kept its word.

li.heading: Settings
li.text: The section "Diplomacy" of the settings has "Favors owed and called in", "Pacts and truces", and "Truces keep raids away" (a hook on the game's choice of raiders, with the deeper game hooks). Off, no debt, pact or truce is made or called in, and those open run out by their terms. Later releases of the diplomacy add their own parts to that section: "Feasts with guests" off, no feast is planned or suggested, and one under way plays out; "Marriage alliances" off, nothing new is matched or offered, a match agreed goes ahead, and a marriage holds. "Ransom", "Envoys" and "Wards and hostages" switch off the parts below; off, nothing new is agreed, and what is under way runs its term. "Council tasks and the keeper of secrets" off (or offices off), no task is set and those under way end, an officer away still comes home, and the keeper neither watches nor sounds anyone out. "Fealty and vassals" off, nothing new is sworn, offered or asked, and the oaths and vassals standing run on. "House renown" off, no house's name is told, read or felt anywhere, and the houses kept are kept. "Against their nature" (with the heart on) off, no act is felt, and what was felt drains as any strain does.

li.heading: Truces
li.text: A truce can be offered to a people at war with the colony when the colony has beaten a raid of theirs in the last 15 days, holds one of their notables or their kin in its cells, or a friend of both has called in a debt for peace. The offer is a letter or a call to their head (their people's card, "Offer a truce"): a season or a year, and a price either way, the colony's silver, theirs, their captives in the colony's cells returned, or a hostage either way for the term. How they take it follows their goodwill, a raid just beaten, one of theirs held, a friend's word, the term and the price. Now and then, after a raid of theirs is beaten, they offer one themselves. Agreed, their envoy walks to the colony's gate under their sign of parley, vouched for by a people at peace with both, and the colony's speaker walks out to them (with the silver when that is the price) and they swear it there. With no such people to vouch for their envoy it is sworn by word, and their answer and their offer say so. When a colonist has sworn vengeance on them, that colonist has their say before the council first, and the council may send the envoy home.

table.li: Age | The colony's word | Their way
Tribal | a peace at the river | green branches carried between camps
Medieval | a truce under a flag | a truce sworn on the hilt
Industrial | a ceasefire | terms signed at a crossing
Spacer | a ceasefire by comms | terms logged and witnessed

li.after: While it holds, the storyteller doesn't send their raids to that home, Rimfolk's own raids keep away, and their raiders' camp near it breaks up. Once per truce their firebrands may raid anyway, one truce in ten (15% for a people of bitter ways), at 0.6 of the game's threat points, and that breaks it, as any raid or ambush of theirs does. At its end it is a peace if their goodwill has come to 0, and runs out otherwise; the people's card says how far their goodwill is from peace.

li.heading: Pacts
li.text: A pact is sworn with a people at peace with the colony at goodwill 20 or more, by a letter or a call to their head ("Propose a pact"), or face to face with one of theirs ("Speak of a pact"); a friend whose head thinks 50 or more of the colony, with an enemy in common, may offer one once a year at most. It runs a year, and at its end they offer to keep it another while they still think well enough of the colony. The Empire makes truces, but keeps its own oaths and makes no pacts. A defense pact: each comes when the other is attacked. A trade pact: each season a trader caravan of theirs comes to the colony, and a cart of the colony's surplus (about 250 silver's worth of the good chosen when it was sworn) is carried out to the gate for their porters, who pay four fifths of its worth in silver.

li.heading: Calling a defense pact in
li.text: While a threat is on a home, "Call them" on their card or the alert makes the call by the colony's means: the caller at a comms console when both sides can use one, else a signal fire laid and lit by the gate where their watchers see it (20 wood, a fire on the hill to a tribe, a beacon for their riders to a medieval people). Their band walks in some hours later, more the further their town, and fights beside the colony. At most once a season a pact; nine times in ten they come, and once their riders are elsewhere. If the attacker is their friend, they decline and the pact ends without blame. Their fallen leave the colony owing them in turn. A debt of honor called in for fighters brings their band the same way.

li.heading: Their call to arms
li.text: When a town of theirs within reach is attacked (a war in the world near it, or with Faction Territories an invasion of it), a defense partner's letter asks the colony for fighters, and so may a people the colony owes a debt of honor. Two of the colony's grown people or more set out by caravan for their town within five days. There the fight is on the game's caravan battle map beside the town, their attackers' band at half the home's threat points against the colony's people and a few of theirs; with Faction Territories its own invasion fight is joined at the town. Arriving keeps the colony's word. Refused, or nobody set out in time, the pact is broken (a debt, refused).

li.heading: Breaking them
li.text: The colony breaks a truce or a pact by attacking that people, their caravans, visitors or towns, or by refusing a call; it may end a pact by letter without blame. Broken by the colony, each people at peace with a town in reach hears that it broke its word. With Factional War, a battle on the colony's land names a pact or truce partner among the two sides: fighting beside a pact partner keeps the pact, and harm done to a truce partner's fighters breaks the truce. A hostage given for the terms pays for a broken word. When their side breaks a truce, their hostage at the colony is the colony's to decide about, by their letter in This week: send them home anyway (their people remember the mercy), keep them (the warden arrests them by the game's own arrest, and their people may then offer a ransom), or ask them to stay if they would; left a few days, they slip away home. When the colony breaks its word, its own hostage is held by their people in the game's own captivity, with the game's ransom demand (or their messenger's), rescue, and in time their joining that people.

li.heading: Ransom for their own
li.text: Two to six days after one of a people is taken prisoner, their messenger may walk to the colony's gate with an offer for them: always for their leader, a notable or a notable's kin, and for anyone else six times in ten from a people at peace and three in ten from one at war with the colony. A people at war sends a go-between of a people at peace with both; with a working comms console and a people who use one, the offer comes as a call. The price is half to the whole of the captive's market value, half again for a notable and twice for their leader, in silver, or in goods from a tribe. "Offer for ransom" on the captive's card writes to their head first, and brings their offer sooner if they want the captive back. Accept, and a warden walks the captive out by the gate while their messenger sets the price down (after a call, their pod brings it). Ask for more, and the colony's speaker bargains: a quarter more, likelier the better their Social, or the messenger walks away. Let the captive go for nothing, and their people owe the colony a debt of honor for it. Keep them, and they may ask once more within a season; refused three times, they hold a grudge and stop asking. A captive paid for leaves no debt of honor, though the game's own goodwill for a captive who leaves healthy stands.

table.li: Age | The colony's word | Their way
Tribal | captives traded back | an exchange of captives for goods
Medieval | ransom by messenger | a price paid in silver
Industrial | ransom by radio | an exchange at a crossing
Spacer | a negotiated exchange by comms | an exchange on agreed terms

li.heading: Ransom for the colony's own
li.text: When another people carries one of the colony's off, the game's own ransom demand comes now and then, at the game's rate, asking 1.2 to 2.2 times the colonist's market value with a day to answer. With a powered comms console it comes as the game's call, as always. Without one, their messenger (or a go-between) brings the same demand to the gate. Paid, the colony's speaker carries the silver out to them, and some hours later the colonist walks in from the edge of the colony's land, or comes by drop pod from a people of the machine ages. A colonist held long may join their captors, as the game has it.

li.heading: Exchanges and the trap
li.text: When a people holds one of the colony's and the colony holds one of theirs, "Offer an exchange" (the captive's card, their people's card, a letter, or face to face with one of theirs at the colony) puts it to them. They agree by who is worth more to them, a notable or their kin counting for more, and their head's regard. Agreed, their party walks the colony's own to the gate, and a warden walks theirs out there. With a people at war with the colony, an exchange at the gate can be a trap: at the game's peace talks' disaster rate, 5%, times the game's own factor for the negotiator's ability (four times with none, 0.4 at its best), a band of theirs at 0.35 of the threat points falls on the gate from its side as the captive walks out. The letter names that chance before the choice, and never with a people at peace.

table.li: The speaker's negotiation ability | Chance of a trap
none | 20%
150% or more | 2%

li.heading: Their envoy for a season
li.text: A people at peace with goodwill 30 or more, whose envoy the colony knows, may offer to send them to live at the colony for a season, at most once a year per people and a season apart at each home, one envoy at a time at a home; the colony may also ask by letter ("Ask for their envoy"). Their envoy comes with an attendant and does no work. They keep about the colony's common rooms by day and indoors in danger, eat at its table (fine meals first), sleep in a bed set aside for them ("Set aside a bed" on their card), else a spare bed or the floor, talk with its people, sit in at a council meeting that falls during the stay, and hand a letter home to their runner at the gate every five days. How the stay goes shows on their card as content, cool or offended, from each day's meals, each night's bed, how their talks with the colonists went, gifts and the meeting; an envoy of the Empire expects a room of their own and fine meals. At the season's end their report moves their head's regard of the colony: up 12 when content, a little when cool, down 10 when offended (and seeing them off early is a slight). A very good stay leaves their people owing the colony a debt of honor. Hurt while here costs a little regard if the colony sheltered them and a lot in the open; hurt by the colony, they leave at once.

table.li: Age | The colony's word | Their way
Tribal | a guest-friend by the fire | a guest-gift and a seat by the fire
Medieval | an envoy at court | letters of credence
Industrial | a consul | credentials presented
Spacer | a liaison | credentials sent ahead by comms

li.after: While their envoy is here, pacts, favors and exchanges can be spoken of face to face, with no letter.

li.heading: The colony's own envoy
li.text: "Send an envoy" on a people's card or one of their towns sends a colonist good with people (Social 6 or more) to live at their town for a season. The council's question says what it costs: their work is lost until they come home, and the road there and back is the world's own. They take food that keeps from the stores, walk to the edge and set out as a caravan of their own. At the town, every five days their letter brings the town's news and its notables think better of the colony, more the better the envoy's Social. At the season's end their hosts give them food for the road, their head a parting gift when they think well of the colony, and they come home better with people. "Call home" on their card brings them back sooner. The settings "Ransom" and "Envoys" in the section "Diplomacy" switch these parts off; what is under way plays out.
